title: The impact of GenAI on jobs, productivity and work organization: a review of the empirical evidence
key_claim: Reviewing experiments, firm-level data, platform studies and representative worker and firm surveys from Australia, Denmark, Germany, Korea, Kuwait, the UK and the US, the ILO finds productivity gains are real albeit often unverified and uneven; large-scale job displacement remains limited; worker-reported time savings of a few per cent of working hours have not yet translated into higher measured output, earnings or employment; and the main risks lie in growing inequalities, erosion of opportunities for younger workers, and the reshaping of how work is organised.
frame_summary: The ILO argues that generative AI's measurable labour-market effect so far is transformation of how work is organised rather than displacement, with productivity gains real but unverified and unevenly distributed.
verbatim_quote: productivity gains are real albeit often unverified and uneven
notes: Tier 1 anchor and the disciplined empirical baseline the organisational-apparatus story runs ahead of. Quote confirmed by hand against the live page at fetch time (2026-07-04T01:04:47Z). title: Workers' exposure to AI: What indicators tell us - and what they don't
date_evidence: visible publication details "Date 17 April 2026" (page metadata: article:published_time 2026-03-02, modified 2026-05-07; the ILO page displays 17 April 2026 as the publication date)
key_claim: AI exposure indicators estimate technological susceptibility, not labour-market outcomes: they rely on static task lists, omit adoption constraints and embed subjective judgements, and 'cannot be interpreted as predictions of job displacement, productivity gains or reskilling needs'; recent capability-based indicators score cognitive, analytical, administrative and managerial occupations as most exposed.
frame_summary: The ILO argues that AI exposure measures are signals of possible job transformation, not forecasts of employment outcomes, and warns against overreading them.
verbatim_quote: cannot be interpreted as predictions of job displacement, productivity gains or reskilling needs
notes: Counter-argument anchor: the evidentiary caution against building institutions on exposure numbers. Quote confirmed by hand against the live page at fetch time (2026-07-04T01:02:13Z). title: Agents are now on the org chart. Who is managing them?
key_claim: CAIO adoption rose from 11% of large enterprises in 2023 to 26% in 2025 (IBM IBV survey of 2,300 organisations), with industry projections of over 40% of the Fortune 500 by end-2026; the HRMS 'employment type' pick list is about to gain an 'AI Agent' entry; a major US enterprise software company describes roughly 3,000 internal AI agents, a 3:1 agent-to-employee ratio, four named worker categories (builders, agent managers, system managers, customer-facing front-liners) and million-dollar salary bands for employees who build or manage AI systems; KPMG argues the CHRO has a structural claim to the Strategy CAIO role.
frame_summary: KPMG argues that AI agents have become workers to be managed, and that HR rather than IT should hold the strategic mandate for the hybrid human-agent workforce.
verbatim_quote: The CIO deploys the agent. HR integrates it as a worker.

title: Deloitte 2026 Global Human Capital Trends press release: In a New Era of Work, Winning Organizations Will Build the Human Advantage
key_claim: Surveying more than 9,000 business and HR leaders across 89 countries, Deloitte finds 65% of organisations believe their culture needs to change significantly because of AI; 60% of executives use AI in decision-making but only 5% say they manage it well; 56% of leaders design AI solely for business outcomes while only 40% design for both business and human outcomes; 66% of C-suite leaders say traditional functions such as HR, finance, IT and legal must change, yet only 7% report progress; neglect accumulates 'culture debt'.
frame_summary: Deloitte argues that work is at a tipping point where organisations must redesign work, governance and culture for human-machine convergence, and that governance and culture lag well behind AI use.
notes: Structural anchor (3-6m band): the canonical annual flagship framing the human-agentic workforce reset; source of the governance-lag quantification.

title: Microsoft Work Trend Index 2026 Shows AI Productivity Is Not Enough
key_claim: Analyst read-through of the 2026 Work Trend Index: 66% of AI users say AI lets them spend more time on high-value work; roughly one in five workers sit in the 'Frontier zone' while about half are in the emergent zone, explaining why AI progress feels uneven inside large companies; 'Frontier Professionals' deliberately do some work without AI to keep skills sharp (43% versus 30% of other users).
frame_summary: Moor Insights argues that individual AI productivity is real but insufficient, and that organisational structure and deliberate skill preservation now separate advanced adopters from the rest.
notes: Independent corroboration of the Work Trend Index findings from outside Microsoft.

title: How Frontier Firms are rebuilding the operating model for the age of AI
key_claim: Drawing on trillions of Microsoft 365 productivity signals and surveys of 20,000 AI-using workers across 10 countries, the 2026 Work Trend Index describes four human-agent collaboration patterns (author, editor, director, orchestrator); organisational factors such as culture, manager support and talent practices account for more than twice the AI impact of individual factors (67% vs 32%); 65% of AI users fear falling behind yet 45% say it feels safer to focus on current goals, and only 13% of workers say they are rewarded for reinventing work with AI.
frame_summary: Microsoft argues that the binding constraint on AI value has moved from individual capability to how firms structure work around human-agent teams, and that leaders must redesign the operating model accordingly.
notes: Vendor research; used as directional corroboration of the human-agent operating-model shift, not as anchor.

title: Employers face a ticking clock under California's AI layoff order
key_claim: California's governor signed an executive order on 21 May 2026 directing state agencies to study AI's labour-market effects, with a 180-day clock on recommendations to revise the Cal-WARN Act; Senate Bill 951 would require 90 days' notice for AI- or automation-driven layoffs at a lowered 25-worker trigger; Connecticut and New York have already amended their WARN laws to require notice when layoffs stem from AI; the Employment Development Department must launch a public dashboard within 90 days tracking AI's effects on employment by sector, and the state must study how union contracts handle AI adoption by 15 October.
frame_summary: HR Executive argues that California's executive order signals imminent AI-specific layoff-notice, severance and reporting obligations, and that HR leaders should audit AI use in employment decisions before the rules land.
notes: Evidence that governments are building their own administrative apparatus (AI-layoff notice categories, dashboards) around the hybrid workforce.
